prompt: Which need pushed most Go projects towards an outside router before Go 1.22?
hint: Look at the first rows of the table.

choices.text: Writing middleware, which `net/http` had no shape for
choices.why: The `func(http.Handler) http.Handler` shape is plain Go and always was.

choices.text: Grouping routes, which needed a framework's router groups
choices.why: A mux mounted inside a mux groups routes, as `/admin/` does.

choices.text: Serving HTTPS, which the standard server lacked
choices.why: TLS is not in the table at all; the gap was routing.

choices.text: Routing by method and reading values out of the path
choices.why: Right. Those rows are closed now by `GET /events` and `{id}`.

prompt: Which of these is still absent from `net/http` and is a real reason a framework helps?
hint: Section 02's second list.

choices.text: Wildcards in a path
choices.why: `{id}` arrived in 1.22.

choices.text: A 405 with an `Allow` header for a wrong method
choices.why: The 1.22 mux writes that by itself.

choices.text: Decoding and validating a body in one call
choices.why: Right. boxoffice needed `decodeJSON` plus a `validate` method for it.

choices.text: Choosing between two overlapping patterns
choices.why: The most specific wins, and a tie panics at registration.

prompt: The lesson says the question is not "does the framework have more". What is the question?
hint: A framework has more, by definition.

choices.text: Whether it is newer than the standard library
choices.why: Age decides nothing here; cost against benefit does.

choices.text: Whether it is faster than `net/http` in a benchmark of hello world
choices.why: Section 08 dismisses that benchmark as evidence about a real service.

choices.text: Whether what it has is worth what it costs
choices.why: Right. Sections 03 and 04 measure each side.

choices.text: Whether the team likes its syntax
choices.why: Taste is not the measure the lesson uses.

prompt: A colleague says: "we need Gin, because the standard library cannot group the `/admin/` routes behind one auth check." What do you answer?
hint: How does boxoffice protect `/admin/`?

choices.text: A wrapped sub-mux at `/admin/` does it
choices.why: Right. That is lesson 2's `requireStaff(tokens)(admin)`.

choices.text: Right: route groups are one of the gaps Go 1.22 left open
choices.why: Groups never needed a framework; that row of the table says "the same".

choices.text: Only by checking the token inside each admin handler
choices.why: The check sits on the subtree, once, not in every handler.

choices.text: Only with `{path...}` and a manual dispatch on the rest of the path
choices.why: Nothing manual is needed; a mounted sub-mux routes the rest.

prompt: How many lines, in total, are boxoffice's seven plumbing files as `wc -l` counted them?
hint: The first `total` line.

prompt: What did those plumbing lines add to boxoffice's `go.mod`?
hint: They use `http.Handler`, `encoding/json` and `context`.

choices.text: One module, `golang.org/x/net`, for CORS
choices.why: CORS is thirty lines of `net/http` in `cors.go`.

choices.text: The validator library behind the `validate` methods
choices.why: The `validate` methods are plain `if` statements.

choices.text: A logging module for `logRequests`
choices.why: It calls `log.Printf` from the standard library.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. `go.mod` lists the module itself and nothing else.

prompt: Which is the strongest argument a framework has against hand-written plumbing, according to section 03?
hint: Think of `decode.go`.

choices.text: It saves the lines of a 25-line `writeJSON`
choices.why: The section calls that hardly an argument.

choices.text: Thousands of users found its bugs
choices.why: Right. The obvious one-line decoder is wrong in four ways.

choices.text: It compiles faster
choices.why: Build time is not the argument.

choices.text: It makes the binary smaller
choices.why: Lesson 4 measured every framework's binary as larger.

prompt: Code written against `net/http` in 2012 still compiles because of the Go ___ compatibility promise.
hint: A version number.

prompt: How many compile errors did the Echo program report when its import was switched from v5 to v4?
hint: Count the lines under `# example.com/fw/echo4`.

prompt: Why did changing only the Echo import line break the file in seven places?
hint: Who owns the handler's signature?

choices.text: v4 needs Go 1.22 and the lab ran an older Go
choices.why: The lab ran Go 1.27.1, and the errors name the context type.

choices.text: `go mod tidy` failed to download v4
choices.why: It downloaded v4.16.0; the build is what failed.

choices.text: The handler's context type changed
choices.why: Right. In v4 `echo.Context` is an interface; in v5 a struct taken by pointer.

choices.text: The sed replaced the import in the wrong file
choices.why: `grep` shows both imports now name v4.

prompt: Your service imports Gin and never calls a function in one of Gin's dependencies. That dependency gets a known vulnerability. Is the service affected?
hint: Section 04 and the tool from `go-production` lesson 9.

choices.text: Yes, until someone checks whether it is reachable and upgrades it
choices.why: Right. The module is in your process; a reachability check and an upgrade settle it.

choices.text: No, a module you never call is never in the binary
choices.why: Gin itself calls its dependencies; code you do not call directly still runs.

choices.text: No, vulnerabilities in indirect dependencies are Gin's responsibility
choices.why: Your service ships it; the responsibility is yours.

choices.text: Yes, and the fix is to remove Gin at once
choices.why: Checking reachability and upgrading is the fix, not a rewrite.

prompt: What happened to `gorilla/mux` in December 2022?
hint: It was the default router of the Go world for years.

choices.text: It was merged into `net/http`
choices.why: The 1.22 patterns were written by the Go team, not merged from gorilla.

choices.text: It released v2 with a new handler type
choices.why: That describes Echo's v5, not gorilla.

choices.text: It was archived, then revived in 2023
choices.why: Right. Every project using it had to decide whether to wait or migrate.

choices.text: It changed its licence
choices.why: The section names archiving, not a licence change.

prompt: Of the costs in section 04, which one does the lesson call the smallest and the easiest to measure?
hint: 31.6 MB against 9.8 MB.

choices.text: The second thing every newcomer has to learn
choices.why: That cost lasts as long as the team changes.

choices.text: A major version that touches every handler
choices.why: Section 04 shows that one in seven errors and calls it expensive.

choices.text: The vulnerabilities that arrive with each module
choices.why: Those need weekly checking; not small.

choices.text: The binary's size
choices.why: Right. It matters a little more in a container image, and is still the smallest.

prompt: A Gin handler starts a goroutine that logs `c.Param("id")` a second later. In tests it logs the right id; under load it logs ids from other customers. Why?
hint: What happens to the context when the handler returns?

choices.text: A data race in the map of events
choices.why: The id comes from the context, not the map.

choices.text: Gin shuffles parameters between routes under load
choices.why: Nothing is shuffled; an object is reused.

choices.text: The logger buffers lines and prints them out of order
choices.why: The ids themselves are wrong, not their order.

choices.text: It needed `c.Copy()`: Gin recycles the original
choices.why: Right. Gin's documentation says to give a goroutine a copy, never the original.

prompt: Lesson 2's `logRequests` middleware has the standard shape. Where does it NOT work unchanged?
hint: Which of these is not `net/http`?

choices.text: Anywhere in Fiber
choices.why: Right. Fiber runs on fasthttp and needs its own middleware or an adaptor.

choices.text: Around a chi router
choices.why: A chi router is an `http.Handler`.

choices.text: Around Echo's engine
choices.why: Echo's engine is an `http.Handler` at the top.

choices.text: Around Gin's engine
choices.why: Around the engine works; inside a route it does not.

prompt: Why does the lesson say a framework's defaults are a bigger surface than `net/http`'s?
hint: Count the places choices are made.

choices.text: `net/http` has no defaults
choices.why: It has some; the missing timeouts are one.

choices.text: Framework defaults change every release
choices.why: The argument is about how many there are.

choices.text: Hundreds of choices against a handful
choices.why: Right. Each of those is found the day a client or auditor finds it.

choices.text: Framework defaults are insecure
choices.why: Each is reasonable for somebody; few are insecure.

prompt: A Gin service must set a header after a middleware has already written, and stream a long response. What does the lesson say happens?
hint: What does `c.JSON` hide?

choices.text: Gin handles both through `c.JSON` options
choices.why: The helper is what has to be bypassed.

choices.text: It cannot be done in Go
choices.why: Lesson 13 streams a response in Go.

choices.text: The service must move to Fiber
choices.why: Nothing about this needs fasthttp.

choices.text: The helper is bypassed and HTTP learnt anyway
choices.why: Right. A framework postpones the day you need HTTP; it does not remove it.

prompt: Twelve developers will write eighty routes, and new people join every month. What does the lesson call the strongest argument for a framework here?
hint: What must every handler look like?

choices.text: Speed under load
choices.why: The routes wait on a database; speed is section 06's other case.

choices.text: Smaller binaries
choices.why: Frameworks made larger binaries in lesson 4.

choices.text: Consistency across every handler
choices.why: Right, and the argument grows with the team.

choices.text: Fewer modules to audit
choices.why: A framework brings more modules, not fewer.

prompt: You like Gin's `binding:"required,max=100"` tags and nothing else about Gin. What does section 06 suggest?
hint: What library sits underneath?

choices.text: Use `go-playground/validator` on its own
choices.why: Right. It is the one part of Gin you can have without Gin.

choices.text: Adopt Gin, because tags only work inside it
choices.why: The validator works on any struct in any handler.

choices.text: Write a tag parser of your own with `reflect`
choices.why: A ready library does this already.

choices.text: Avoid tags; they are slower than `if` statements
choices.why: The lesson weighs readability and mistakes, not speed.

prompt: A team wants Fiber "because it is faster". The service answers every request after a PostgreSQL query. What does the lesson ask for before agreeing?
hint: Where does the time go?

choices.text: A hello-world benchmark comparing Fiber and `net/http`
choices.why: That measures a service nobody runs.

choices.text: Nothing; Fiber is faster, so it is the better choice
choices.why: Speed nobody notices does not pay for leaving `net/http`.

choices.text: A count of the modules Fiber brings
choices.why: That is a cost, not evidence that the speed matters.

choices.text: A profile of the real service under its real load
choices.why: Right. With a database behind each request, halving the HTTP share is not noticed.

prompt: All of your team's services are written in Echo. You are starting a new one. What does the lesson recommend?
hint: The least technical reason.

choices.text: Echo
choices.why: Right. Shared knowledge and middleware beat any difference in the table.

choices.text: The standard library, the course's default
choices.why: The team question comes first and overrides the default.

choices.text: chi, as a compromise between the two
choices.why: A lone service in another style costs everyone who touches it.

choices.text: Gin, because more people know it
choices.why: The people who matter here already know Echo.

prompt: What is the lesson's test for telling a library from a framework?
hint: Look at one function's parameters.

choices.text: Whether it is in the standard library
choices.why: chi is outside it and counts as a library.

choices.text: Whether the handler's signature stays `func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request)`
choices.why: Right. A library leaves the shape of your program alone.

choices.text: Whether it has more than ten modules
choices.why: Module count is a cost, not the definition.

choices.text: Whether it ships middleware
choices.why: chi ships middleware and is still a library.

prompt: How many modules besides the program's own did `go list -m all` print for the chi version?
hint: The last command of the build.

prompt: The chi version answered `DELETE /events/1`. How did its answer differ from `ServeMux`'s?
hint: Compare the `Allow` headers.

choices.text: Its 405 listed only `GET` and had no body
choices.why: Right. `ServeMux` adds `HEAD` and writes `Method Not Allowed`.

choices.text: It answered 404 instead of 405
choices.why: It answered 405; that is Gin's 404.

choices.text: It answered with an HTML page
choices.why: That was Beego, in lesson 4.

choices.text: Its 405 came back as JSON
choices.why: That was Echo; chi's had an empty body.

prompt: boxoffice needs rate limiting. Which choice keeps to the middle path?
hint: Each piece replaceable on its own.

choices.text: `x/time/rate` in a standard middleware
choices.why: Right. A small package, in the shape lesson 2 uses.

choices.text: Move to Echo, which ships a rate limiter
choices.why: That changes every handler to get one middleware.

choices.text: A counter in each handler, compared against a constant
choices.why: Work for every request belongs in a middleware, once.

choices.text: Nothing; rate limiting needs a framework
choices.why: Section 07 names a library for it.

prompt: Match each gap of section 02 to the middle-path answer section 07 gives.
hint: Each piece in the standard shape.

prompt: Put section 08's four questions in the order the lesson asks them.
hint: The first yes ends the search.
items: Does the team already have a framework?
Has a measurement shown the HTTP layer is where the time goes?
Will many people write many routes that must all look the same?
Does `ServeMux` lack a routing feature you need?
trap: The team question comes first because it overrides all the others.

prompt: Six months into a standard-library service, the same twenty lines of decoding and error handling are pasted into every handler and are drifting apart. What does section 08 read in that?
hint: A sign of a wrong choice, and what to do.

choices.text: Write the helper now, or adopt one that has it
choices.why: Right, and the fix is cheapest early.

choices.text: Nothing: duplication is the normal price of the standard library
choices.why: The section names exactly this as a sign.

choices.text: A sign the team needs Fiber
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with pasted code.

choices.text: A reason to rewrite the service in another language
choices.why: One helper settles it.

prompt: Which is section 08's sign that adopting a framework was the wrong choice?
hint: Where does the team's time go?

choices.text: Half the time goes into overriding its defaults
choices.why: Right. Both mean the framework's shape costs more than it saves.

choices.text: The binary is larger than the standard library's
choices.why: That is known on day one and is the smallest cost.

choices.text: A new developer needs a day to learn it
choices.why: A day is cheap; the section names larger signs.

choices.text: It has a GitHub issue open
choices.why: Every active project has open issues.

prompt: For which of these new services does section 08 end at the standard library? Choose all that apply.
hint: All four answers must be no.

choices.text: A solo developer's six-route API, no framework around it, no measured bottleneck, no special routing
choices.why: Right. Four noes.

choices.text: A new service in a team whose other services all use Gin
choices.why: Question 1 says yes: use Gin.

choices.text: An internal API of a small team, waiting on PostgreSQL, routes like `/events/{id}`
choices.why: Right. Nothing there needs more than 1.22's patterns.

choices.text: A service needing `{id:[0-9]+}` patterns
choices.why: Question 4 says yes: add a router such as chi.

prompt: A public API product needs an OpenAPI document that stays in step with eighty routes, and the company has no framework yet. Which answer follows the lesson?
hint: Section 06 says this alone can decide.

choices.text: Hand-write the OpenAPI file and keep the standard library
choices.why: A hand-written description drifts from the code.

choices.text: Fiber, because public APIs need speed
choices.why: No profile was mentioned; the need is the document.

choices.text: chi, because it generates OpenAPI
choices.why: chi is a router; section 07 says it does routing and middleware.

choices.text: Adopt one that generates it from the code
choices.why: Right. When the API is a product, that alone can decide.

prompt: Why does the lesson call the choice of framework one of the few decisions in a Go service that is expensive to reverse?
hint: Where does the framework appear in the code?

choices.text: Frameworks charge licence fees to leave
choices.why: Every framework here is free.

choices.text: Its modules cannot be removed from `go.sum`
choices.why: `go mod tidy` removes unused modules.

choices.text: The binary keeps its code after you stop importing it
choices.why: A rebuild drops what is not imported.

choices.text: It is in the signature of every handler
choices.why: Right. Changing it touches every route, as Echo's v4 build showed.
